blocks.title: Impact of an outage
blocks.question: If this service stopped tomorrow morning, what would it concretely change for you?
blocks.help: Look at what actually breaks: customers who can no longer order, a team that can no longer work, a damaged reputation.

blocks.title: Overlap with other services
blocks.question: Do other services or applications in your organization do the same thing or something similar?
blocks.help: Look for overlapping features or code doing the same job elsewhere in your organization.

blocks.title: Service availability constraints
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure

options.label: 24/7 availability, with a 99.99% commitment and international coverage

answers.0.3: 1 - 7 days a week, 24 hours a day - 99.99% - International coverage

options.label: 24/7 availability, with a 99% commitment

answers.0.3: 2 - 7 days a week, 24 hours a day - 99%

options.label: Some service commitments, no permanent availability requirement
Business-hours availability only, no service commitment, no disaster recovery plan

answers.0.3: 4 - 5 days a week, 8 hours a day - No SLA - No Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP)

options.label: No availability commitment

blocks.question: What availability constraints apply to your service?
blocks.help: Uptime commitments, disaster recovery plans, guaranteed operating hours. Strict constraints reduce the opportunities to modify, migrate or optimize the infrastructure.

blocks.title: Connections with other systems
blocks.question: How many other systems is this service technically connected to?
blocks.help: Count the active connections: APIs you call, shared databases, authentication services, incoming or outgoing data flows.

blocks.title: Source code availability
blocks.question: To what extent do you have access to this service's source code?
blocks.help: Code fully accessible to the team, code open to the public, closed code provided by a vendor, or limited access to certain modules only.

blocks.title: Team's command of the service
blocks.question: Does your team know this service well enough to modify it with full confidence?
blocks.help: Look at whether the team masters the functional and technical design, whether it can work calmly or only cautiously, or whether knowledge is too fragmented.

blocks.title: Architecture complexity
blocks.question: How would you rate the complexity of this service's architecture?
blocks.help: Think about the number of components, their interactions, the different technologies used, and how easy it is to understand how the whole thing works.

blocks.title: Infrastructure size
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: How large is this service's infrastructure compared to your other services?
blocks.help: Compare the number and size of servers, virtual machines, containers or other hosted components with what you have elsewhere in the organization.

blocks.title: Stored data volume
blocks.interviewee: the person who manages the data
blocks.question: How much data does this service store compared to your other services?
blocks.help: Look at databases, files, archives, backups. Compare with what you have elsewhere in the organization.

blocks.title: Service complexity
blocks.question: How would you describe the complexity of this service?
blocks.help: Think about the number of features, business rules, and the different use cases you handle.

blocks.title: User experience smoothness
blocks.question: How do you rate the smoothness and intuitiveness of the user journeys?
blocks.help: Look at what your users say, where they get stuck, and the improvements on your waiting list.

blocks.title: Legacy devices
blocks.question: Does this service work well on the oldest devices your users still use?
blocks.help: Check for slowdowns, incompatibilities, or whether the experience remains comfortable.

blocks.title: Known performance issues
blocks.question: Does your backlog contain performance issues or optimization needs?
blocks.help: Open tickets about service slowness, recurring discussions about efficiency, technical improvements identified but not yet handled.

blocks.title: Feature effectiveness
blocks.question: Are this service's main features well implemented and performant?
blocks.help: Look for features that duplicate each other or could be more efficient.

blocks.title: Data deletion and archiving
blocks.interviewee: the person who manages the data
blocks.question: Do you have a data deletion and archiving policy for this service?
blocks.help: Look for formalized rules, whether they are applied consistently, whether automations are in place, and whether regular checks verify their enforcement.

blocks.title: Service hosting country
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: In which country is your service hosted?
blocks.help: The hosting country determines the carbon intensity of the electricity mix used by your servers. This information is normally collected automatically, but you can fill it in if needed.

blocks.title: Ease of observing behavior
blocks.question: Is it easy to set up and operate tools to track this service's behavior in production?
blocks.help: Think about the ability to add metrics, logs, traces, alerts, dashboards. Look at whether tools are already in place and whether they are easy to evolve.

blocks.title: Ease of code reviews
blocks.question: Is it easy to organize code reviews or pair programming on this project?
blocks.help: Look at whether processes are already in place, whether the team has the time and habits for it, and whether organizational or technical obstacles complicate putting them in place.

blocks.title: Ease of setting up CI/CD
blocks.question: Is it easy to set up or evolve an automated build and deployment process for this project?
blocks.help: Look at whether automations already exist, whether the infrastructure allows it, and whether the team has the skills and access needed to build and test the code automatically.

blocks.title: Ease of adding tests
blocks.question: Is it easy to add or evolve automated tests on this project?
blocks.help: Think unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end tests. Look at whether a test infrastructure already exists, whether the code lends itself to testing, and whether the team has the skills and time to write tests.

blocks.title: Ease of changing the technical layer
blocks.question: Is it easy to modify the technical aspects of this service without touching the functional code?
blocks.help: Look at whether the business code is well separated from the technical integration. For example, can you change database, authentication service or framework without rewriting the functional logic?

blocks.title: Ease of tracking quality
blocks.question: Is it easy to set up and track quality indicators for this software?
blocks.help: Think code coverage, complexity, number of bugs, time to change, deployment frequency. Look at whether tools already exist or are easy to add.

blocks.title: Ease of documenting the project
blocks.question: Is it easy to maintain complete and up-to-date documentation for this project?
blocks.help: Look at whether documentation already exists, whether the team has the tools and time to keep it up to date, and whether the project lends itself to it. Think architecture, development guides, explanations of technical choices.

blocks.title: Ease of removing duplication
blocks.question: Is it easy to spot and remove duplicated code in this project?
blocks.help: Look at whether copy-pasted code or repeated logic exists, whether the team has the tools to detect it, and whether the architecture allows factoring it out without risk.

blocks.title: Autonamey to deploy tools
blocks.question: Is it easy for your team to deploy the tools it needs to observe, measure and optimize this system?
blocks.help: Look at whether the team can install custom tools, access performance data, and use platform-provided tools, without having to request heavy authorizations.

blocks.title: Main journeys and screens

options.label: Short journeys with few steps AND light screens with essential information only
Short journeys with few steps BUT heavy screens (lots of content, heavy media)
Long or redundant journeys BUT light screens
Long or redundant journeys AND heavy screens

blocks.question: How are your main user journeys organized, and what is displayed on screen?
blocks.help: Count the steps needed to perform common actions, and look at how much information and media you display on the most visited screens.

blocks.title: Test environments
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure

options.label: Reduced infrastructure AND reduced databases
Reduced infrastructure BUT databases as large as in production
Infrastructure identical to production BUT reduced databases
Infrastructure AND databases identical to production
We have no test environments

blocks.question: How large are your test environments compared to production?
blocks.help: Look at the number and size of your virtual machines, containers, and the volume of your databases.

blocks.title: Added value of digital
blocks.question: Have you identified a non-digital solution and shown that your digital version brings clear added value?
blocks.help: Look for time savings, accessibility gains, or reduced material impact compared to what existed before.

blocks.title: Knowledge of users
blocks.question: Do you document the needs, usage contexts and devices of your target users?
blocks.help: Look for personas, interviews, usage analyses, or a list of commonly used devices.

blocks.title: Impact of updates
blocks.question: Do you test that your new features remain performant on old or modest devices, and do you offer lightweight modes when needed?
blocks.help: Look at whether you really test on these devices, and whether you offer a simplified mode when performance drops.

blocks.title: Native or custom components
blocks.question: Do you use the system's native components, or do you justify each custom component by a real need?
blocks.help: The system's buttons, menus and forms are more performant and accessible than custom-built ones, except with justification.

blocks.title: Automatic media playback
blocks.question: Are your animations, videos, sounds or maps only started when the user asks for them?
blocks.help: Check that no content starts on its own, or that autoplay is truly necessary, optimized and controllable.

blocks.title: Adaptation to hardware
blocks.question: Does your application detect low-spec devices and automatically switch to a lightweight mode?
blocks.help: For example: reduced image quality, simplified rendering, or automatic disabling of heavy features.

blocks.title: Usefulness of features
blocks.question: Is each feature of your service actually used and does it bring value?
blocks.help: Look at your usage analytics and user feedback, and check whether you have removed redundant or unused features.

blocks.title: Testing on legacy devices

options.label: We test on the oldest devices in our target range, and no compatibility issue was detected
We detected compatibility issues, but the service remains usable on these devices
We detected compatibility issues that really degrade the experience on these devices
Our service does not target any old devices: the user base is recent and controlled

blocks.question: What happens when you test your service on the oldest devices you commit to supporting?
blocks.help: That is, the devices you promise to support, even if they are several years old.
blocks.note: The scope of targeted devices is a product decision: to be validated with the product manager.

blocks.title: Low-bandwidth compatibility
blocks.question: Does your application remain usable on a low-speed connection, thanks to optimized requests, lightened files and caching?
blocks.help: Look at whether you limit the number and size of requests, whether you reduce images and videos, and whether you cache content.

blocks.title: Dark patterns
blocks.question: Does your design avoid practices that artificially push the user to consume more?
blocks.help: Look for infinite scroll, forced autoplay, hidden unsubscribes, pre-checked boxes.

blocks.title: Frugal default settings
blocks.question: Are your default settings frugal, and can users easily adjust them?
blocks.help: Look at the number of items displayed, media quality, and refresh frequency.

blocks.title: Limiting trackers
blocks.question: Do you limit the number of trackers to the strict minimum, and is each tracking tool justified?
blocks.help: Marketing and analytics tools are often responsible for a third of the traffic: remove the redundant ones.
blocks.note: The justification for each tracker is a product or marketing decision: to be validated with the product manager.

blocks.title: Usage frequency
blocks.question: Does this service see regular and significant use?
blocks.help: Check that the usage frequency is proportionate to what the service costs in resources.

blocks.title: User volume
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Does the volume of active users justify the architecture and resources allocated?
blocks.help: Look at whether the number of users is proportionate to the size of your infrastructure.

blocks.title: Resource-hungry technologies
blocks.question: Does your tech stack avoid particularly resource-hungry technologies, or do you justify them?
blocks.help: For example: generative AI, proof-of-work blockchain, or other technologies known for their consumption.

blocks.title: Compatibility strategy
blocks.question: Have you defined a compatibility strategy for your users' devices?
blocks.help: Check whether you have a list of targeted devices, whether you run compatibility tests, and whether you support legacy devices.

blocks.title: Communication between components
blocks.question: Are your components loosely coupled, and does their communication cause no slowdowns or unnecessary complexity?
blocks.help: Look at whether one component can change without breaking the others, and whether their communication is fast and reliable.

blocks.title: Smoothing load peaks
blocks.question: Do you smooth your load peaks by deferring tasks that do not need to run immediately?
blocks.help: For example: process exports or notifications in batches, or use queues to spread the work.

blocks.title: Caching
blocks.question: Do you cache the results of your costly computations and queries when they are reused several times?
blocks.help: Look at whether you recompute the same things several times, or whether you keep the result in memory to reuse it.

blocks.title: Cost optimization
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Have you put in place a strategy to optimize your infrastructure costs?
blocks.help: For example: spot underused components, right-size them, or switch to better-sized services.

blocks.title: Environmental impact monitoring
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Do you monitor the environmental impact of your infrastructure?
blocks.help: For example: carbon emissions of your servers, energy efficiency and water consumption of your datacenter.

blocks.title: Regional electricity mix
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Have you chosen a hosting region whose electricity mix has a low impact?
blocks.help: Regions where electricity is decarbonized, such as France, Norway or Iceland, have a much lower impact.

blocks.title: Shared infrastructure
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Is your infrastructure shared?
blocks.help: For example: virtual machines, containers, or managed services that share resources with other projects.

blocks.title: Sizing and elasticity
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure

options.label: Our components run at at least 70% CPU or RAM load, and bounded auto-scaling is in place (or load is constant)
Our components run at at least 70% load, but there is no auto-scaling while load varies
Our components run below 70% load, but bounded auto-scaling is in place (or load is constant)
Our components run below 70% load, and there is no auto-scaling while load varies

blocks.question: Do your components run at at least 70% load, and does their number adjust when the load varies?
blocks.help: Look at the CPU or memory load of your servers and containers. Automatic scaling must have an upper bound to avoid runaway costs.

blocks.title: Shutting down environments
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Do you shut down your non-production environments when nobody is using them?
blocks.help: For example: development or test environments switched off at night, on weekends, or between test campaigns.

blocks.title: Handling of old data
blocks.interviewee: the person who manages the data

options.label: Automatic deletion and archiving mechanisms are applied, AND rarely accessed data has already been moved to cold storage
Automatic deletion and archiving mechanisms are applied, but everything stays on primary storage
No automatic mechanism, but rarely accessed data has already been moved to cold storage
No automatic mechanism, everything stays on primary storage

blocks.question: What happens when a piece of data becomes useless or rarely accessed?
blocks.help: For example: a rule that automatically deletes or archives old invoices, or a move to a slower but less energy-intensive disk for rarely requested data.
blocks.note: Whether slower access is acceptable for the user is a product decision: to be validated with the product manager.

blocks.title: Database optimization
blocks.question: Do you have a strategy to optimize your databases' performance?
blocks.help: For example: choose the right indexes, model tables to limit costly queries, clean the database regularly.

blocks.title: Suitable storage technologies
blocks.question: Do your storage technologies really match what you do with them?
blocks.help: For example: a classic relational database for structured data, a document-oriented database for flexible content, a column store for analytics, or a specialized database for specific cases.

blocks.title: Data duplication
blocks.interviewee: the person who manages the data
blocks.question: Have you spotted duplicated data and checked whether it is intentional?
blocks.help: Some duplication is useful: to keep the service accessible even in case of an outage, or to speed up certain queries. Other duplication is accidental and wastes space for nothing.

blocks.title: What your tools revealed

options.label: Both practices are in place and revealed no efficiency problem
Static analysis revealed nothing, but the load-testing campaign revealed problems, or we don't run one
Static analysis revealed possible gains, or we don't run it, but the load-testing campaign revealed nothing
Both revealed problems, or at least one of the two practices is missing

blocks.question: Did your code analysis tools and load tests reveal points to improve?
blocks.help: Automatic code analysis tools and high-load tests help detect inefficiencies. The absence of these practices also counts as improvement potential.

blocks.title: Optimization backlog
blocks.question: Does your backlog contain optimization tasks?
blocks.help: For example: tickets or issues aimed at speeding up a page, reducing memory consumption, or improving response time.

blocks.title: Performance indicators
blocks.question: Do your current performances match what you aim for?
blocks.help: For example: page load time, API response time, number of requests processed per second.
blocks.note: The project's performance ambition is a product decision: to be validated with the product manager.

blocks.title: Optimization of frequent journeys
blocks.question: Have the most frequent user journeys been studied for optimization?
blocks.help: Look at whether you have analyzed and improved the most traveled code paths.

blocks.title: Up-to-date tech stack and dependencies

options.label: The base is at least on the latest LTS AND the main dependencies are up to date
The base is at least on the latest LTS, but important dependencies are outdated
The base is behind the latest LTS, but the main dependencies are up to date
The base is outdated AND important dependencies are too

blocks.question: Are your platform and main libraries up to date?
blocks.help: The platform is for example Node, Python, Java, PHP: check that you are at least on the version the publisher commits to maintaining long-term. Libraries are the frameworks and modules you import into your code.

blocks.title: Component configuration
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Have you checked whether your components could be better configured?
blocks.help: For example: tuning the Java virtual machine settings, database connection pools, or a server's memory limits.

blocks.title: Service user interface
blocks.question: Does your service have a user interface that people interact with directly?
blocks.discarded_label: No, this is a service without an interface (API, batch, worker, compute service, etc.)
blocks.applicable_label: Yes, the service has a user interface (web, mobile, desktop, etc.)
blocks.help: A user interface includes screens, buttons, forms, web pages. A service that only exposes an API to other programs has no user interface.

blocks.title: Service data storage
blocks.interviewee: the person who manages the data
blocks.question: Does your service keep data in a database or storage of its own?
blocks.discarded_label: No, the service retains no data (or only in temporary cache)
blocks.applicable_label: Yes, the service retains persistent data (database, files, etc.)
blocks.help: Persistent data is kept even after the service restarts. A temporary in-memory cache is not persistent storage.

blocks.title: Test environments
blocks.interviewee: the person who operates the infrastructure
blocks.question: Do you have test or development environments separate from production?
blocks.discarded_label: No, we do not have a separate test environment
blocks.applicable_label: Yes, we have test or development environments
blocks.help: A test environment is a separate infrastructure where you can test your changes before deploying them to production.
